children.text: Childhood Displacement, the Antonio Maceo Brigade, and the Meanings of Returning to Cuba
Return as a Historical and Personal Question

The institutions examined in the preceding section provided spaces through which Cuban migrants in Puerto Rico organized social relationships, preserved cultural practices, and articulated particular understandings of their country's past. Yet the meanings attached to Cuba did not necessarily remain confined to the traditions or political positions sustained by these associations. For migrants and their descendants, the possibility of visiting the island could raise questions that institutional memory alone could not resolve. Returning might involve the recovery of family relationships, an encounter with places remembered since childhood, or the reconsideration of political convictions developed after migration. These possibilities became especially consequential when young Cuban emigrants began challenging the assumption that departure required an enduring separation from the country they had left.
The documentary
55 hermanos

(1978), directed by Jesús Díaz and produced by the Instituto Cubano del Arte e Industria Cinematográficos (ICAIC), provides a particularly significant audiovisual perspective on these questions. Its first part documents the return to Cuba of the initial fifty-five participants in the Antonio Maceo Brigade, a group of young emigrants whose experiences of displacement and political socialization differed from those of many members of the earlier exile generation. Through scenes of arrival, family reunification, recollections of childhood, and reflections on life in the United States, the documentary presents return as an encounter between remembered experiences and a country that participants could again visit physically. Its historical significance lies not only in recording the journey, but also in showing how personal attachments and political interpretations became intertwined in the participants' accounts of their lives.
These images require attention to the circumstances of their production. As an ICAIC documentary,
55 hermanos

represents the encounters through choices of filming, interviewing, editing, and narrative organization. Its presentation of emotional reunions and political reflections cannot be treated as an exhaustive account of the Brigade or as evidence that every participant understood the visit identically. Nevertheless, the testimonies offer access to experiences that complicate representations of Cuban migration exclusively through ideological opposition. Read alongside Natalia Bonilla's
Ecos del Exilio

(2013), produced decades later in the context of Cuban life in Puerto Rico, the film makes it possible to examine how return acquired different meanings across generations, geographical settings, and historical moments.
Nostalgia, Childhood Memory, and the Materiality of Return
One of the most striking sequences in the first part of
55 hermanos

concerns the arrival of the Brigade's participants in Cuba. As they descend from the airplane, some cry while others join in singing the Cuban national anthem. The scene brings together gestures of personal emotion and a recognizable symbol of national belonging. Tears, collective singing, and the physical act of entering Cuban territory become part of the film's representation of return. Yet these gestures do not necessarily communicate identical meanings. For individual participants, the arrival could involve anticipation, familiarity, uncertainty, or the emotional consequences of prolonged separation. The documentary presents their encounter as a public moment while preserving expressions that point toward distinct biographical experiences.

The participants' descriptions of what they missed about Cuba provide another dimension of this encounter. Their memories turn repeatedly toward landscapes, the sea, childhood homes, schools, animals, and familiar places associated with everyday life before departure. One interviewee explains that the desire to see his country again had become difficult to endure while living abroad. Others describe their longing for particular environments or their wish to revisit places connected to childhood activities. Such recollections suggest that attachment to Cuba did not depend exclusively on a consciously articulated political position. It could also persist through remembered sensations, routines, relationships, and geographical surroundings whose significance developed during years of absence.

The distinction between remembering a place and encountering it again becomes central to the historical interpretation of these accounts. Childhood memories preserve selective impressions of environments that may have changed substantially by the time of return. Visiting a former school or home can therefore involve both recognition and confrontation with temporal distance. The landscape encountered in the present is not necessarily identical to the one preserved in memory, even when familiar details allow the visitor to reconnect with an earlier experience. The physical journey does not eliminate that distance. Instead, it makes the relationship between remembered and present places available to reconsideration.

The sea offers a particularly suggestive example. Within the participants' recollections, its significance cannot be reduced to its geographical presence. As a remembered element of Cuban surroundings, it belongs to an intimate relationship with the environment in which childhood unfolded. The desire to see it again illustrates how migration can transform ordinary features of a landscape into objects of longing. In this sense, nostalgia operates through material references: a school, a house, an animal, a familiar view. Their importance emerges from the relationships and experiences with which they are associated rather than from an intrinsic or universally shared meaning.

These scenes also complicate the assumption that nostalgia necessarily implies a desire to resume permanent residence in the country of origin. The wish to revisit a familiar place and the decision to establish one's future there are distinct matters. Returning physically may satisfy a desire for contact while simultaneously revealing transformations that make the past impossible to recover in its previous form. The testimonies collected in
55 hermanos
allow us to investigate this distinction without determining in advance what the journey meant for every participant.
Family Separation: Protection, Fear, and the Experience of Abandonment

The documentary's attention to childhood extends beyond memories of familiar places. Participants also recount the circumstances under which they left Cuba, including fears surrounding parental authority and the possibility that children would be separated from their families. Some testimonies refer to the
patria potestad

controversy, while others describe the emotional consequences of departure from the position of children who did not necessarily understand the political circumstances determining their futures. These accounts bring a significant tension into view: a decision interpreted by parents as an effort to protect their children could be experienced differently by those children themselves.
The broader historical circumstances of the
patria potestad
controversy were examined earlier in this essay through the distinction between political misinformation and parental decisions made under uncertainty. The relevance of
55 hermanos

is different. Rather than returning to the origins of the rumor, the documentary allows us to consider how participants later interpreted childhood experiences shaped by the fears and decisions of adults. Some accounts describe feelings of abandonment, suggesting that the purposes attributed to migration by parents did not necessarily determine how their children understood separation. Their recollections do not establish the experiences of all children who emigrated during this period, but they demonstrate why parental intentions and children's responses must remain analytically distinct.

The film's reunification scenes bring the temporal consequences of migration into particularly visible form. Relatives encounter one another after separations that, in some cases, had lasted approximately twenty years. These meetings place individuals whose relationships originated in an earlier family life within circumstances transformed by time and distance. Reunification therefore involves more than the restoration of physical proximity. Participants must encounter people whose lives have continued in their absence, while confronting the accumulated experiences that cannot be recovered simply by meeting again.

Such encounters also expose the limits of interpreting migration exclusively through the distinction between voluntary and forced departure. Children who left as a consequence of parental decisions occupied a different position from the adults responsible for those choices. Their subsequent experiences of education, cultural adaptation, and family separation could lead them to develop interpretations that diverged from the explanations originally offered by their parents. The memories articulated in
55 hermanos
demonstrate how departure could remain a contested event within the same family's history, even when its members continued to share attachments to one another.
Growing Up in the United States: Adaptation, Political Socialization, and Disagreement
Several participants in
55 hermanos

connect their changing understandings of Cuba to the experiences they encountered while growing up in the United States. Their testimonies refer to difficulties of cultural adaptation, rejection or discomfort associated with aspects of American society, and the tensions involved in being expected to understand their departure primarily through the language of rescue from communism. For some, that narrative did not adequately account for their continuing affection for Cuba or the personal costs of family separation. The problem was not simply whether they accepted or rejected a political explanation of migration, but whether that explanation allowed room for experiences that did not fit its expected emotional and ideological terms.

The documentary also records participants discussing the influence of American education, the Civil Rights Movement, and opposition to the Vietnam War on their political development. These experiences became important points of reference through which some young emigrants reconsidered established interpretations of Cuba and the relationship between their country of origin and the United States. Their political perspectives therefore developed not exclusively through memories inherited from Cuba, but also through encounters with social movements and debates taking place in the society where they had established their lives.

This dimension complicates any straightforward opposition between adaptation to American society and continued attachment to Cuba. Political experiences acquired in the United States could provide resources for questioning interpretations of Cuban history received within exile communities. Engagement with struggles over racial equality, civil rights, and American military intervention did not necessarily lead all participants toward identical political positions. Within the testimonies presented in the documentary, however, these experiences form part of the explanations some young emigrants offer for their reconsideration of the country they left.

The formation of the Antonio Maceo Brigade becomes intelligible within this intersection of personal memories and political socialization. Its participants did not simply reproduce their parents' understanding of departure, nor did their decision to return erase the consequences of migration. Instead, some developed interpretations shaped by childhood displacement, education abroad, encounters with political movements, and the desire to establish renewed relationships with Cuba. The possibility of returning consequently became a means of acting upon those interpretations rather than only expressing nostalgia for a remembered past.
The Antonio Maceo Brigade and the Political Meanings of Reconnection

The first visit of the Antonio Maceo Brigade in December 1977 transformed the possibility of return into an organized encounter. The journey brought fifty-five young Cuban emigrants to the island with the authorization of the Cuban government, creating opportunities for family reunification and renewed contact with places associated with their earlier lives. The formation of the Brigade also expressed a political challenge to the idea that Cuban emigrants necessarily shared an enduring position of opposition to renewed relations with the island. Yet the initiative did not erase the diversity of political perspectives among Cubans living abroad or establish that reconciliation had been achieved.
In
Ecos del Exilio

, Ana María reflects on her participation in the Brigade and places this experience within a longer account of migration, family history, and political disagreement (Bonilla 00:31:12–00:35:49). Her intervention is particularly significant because the documentary also includes an earlier account in which she recalls the fears that influenced her family's departure from Cuba. The relationship between these testimonies makes visible the possibility that an individual can recognize the circumstances shaping an earlier generation's decisions while developing a different relationship to the country those decisions required leaving.

The comparison between Díaz's film and Ana María's later account requires distinguishing their different historical and audiovisual positions.
55 hermanos
was produced close to the initial encounter and presents the participants within a documentary narrative centered on reconnection.
Ecos del Exilio

, by contrast, places Ana María's recollections among accounts of displacement, political conflict, and generational differences in Puerto Rico. The same historical initiative thus enters two audiovisual narratives organized around different questions. Neither film should be treated as a transparent record independent of its conditions of production.

This distinction is consequential for understanding community memory. The earlier film foregrounds a generation of young emigrants who sought contact with Cuba through an organized initiative, while the later documentary preserves retrospective interpretations shaped by the decades that followed. Reading them together reveals how return can become part of different narratives about migration without requiring these narratives to coincide. The Brigade's history belongs both to the experiences of its participants and to the subsequent public interpretations through which those experiences have been remembered.
Visiting Cuba, Inherited Convictions, and the Limits of Political Consensus
The political meanings of return also emerge in another sequence of
Ecos del Exilio

, when Ricardo Nieves questions why the experiences and convictions of older relatives should prevent him from visiting Cuba. Born in Puerto Rico and identified as a third-generation descendant, Ricardo acknowledges the significance of his family's history while considering a relationship with Cuba that might differ from the positions inherited from his parents and grandparents (Bonilla 00:14:51–00:16:15). His reflections do not replicate the circumstances of the young emigrants who joined the Antonio Maceo Brigade. Nevertheless, the comparison reveals a recurring tension between recognition of earlier experiences and the desire to develop an independent relationship with the island.
Ricardo Nieves: Family Memory and the Possibility of Visiting Cuba. Existing AVAnnotate annotation.

The historical distance between these accounts is essential. The Brigade's participants had experienced childhood in Cuba before developing their political perspectives abroad, whereas Ricardo approaches the possibility of visiting from a life formed in Puerto Rico. Their relationships to Cuba therefore differ in biographical origin, generational position, and historical circumstances. What connects them analytically is not a shared experience of displacement, but the question of whether earlier political divisions should determine the conditions of subsequent contact.

The possibility of visiting Cuba also raises questions about the relationship between family acceptance and institutional permission. Ricardo's reference to a special permit identifies travel as subject to formal requirements, while his concern with his relatives' expectations introduces the pressures surrounding decisions that carry political meaning within a family. Neither form of authorization is equivalent to the other. Legal permission may make a journey possible without resolving disagreements about whether it should occur; family approval may provide emotional support without determining the conditions established by governments. The desire to return consequently develops within overlapping relationships of authority, obligation, and personal judgment.
Returning to a Place and Being Recognized as Belonging
The encounter between remembered and present Cuba does not necessarily resolve the question of belonging. A later sequence of
Ecos del Exilio

introduces this problem through Jay Martínez, who expresses a longing to return while describing uncertainty about being recognized as belonging either in Cuba or in Puerto Rico (Bonilla 00:47:09–00:49:01). His account complicates the assumption that renewed physical contact with a place necessarily restores the relationship that existed before migration. A person may retain a strong attachment to a country while encountering social judgments that question the legitimacy or character of that connection.
Jay Martínez: Longing for Return and the Limits of Recognition. Existing AVAnnotate annotation.
Read against the arrival scenes of
55 hermanos

, Martínez's reflections make visible two dimensions of return that should not be collapsed. The earlier documentary foregrounds the emotional force of encountering Cuba after years of separation. Martínez's later testimony raises a different question: whether returning or wishing to return can overcome the distance created by emigration and changing social relationships. The recognition he seeks cannot be secured through geographical movement alone. It depends partly on how others understand his connection to the places with which he identifies.

The comparison also clarifies why return cannot be interpreted as the simple recovery of an earlier identity. Migration transforms the circumstances within which relationships to place develop. Memories acquire new meanings, individuals encounter different social environments, and the places once known continue to change during their absence. Physical return can therefore create an additional experience of Cuba without erasing the histories formed elsewhere. For Cubans who established their lives in Puerto Rico, the question of belonging involved these intersecting relationships rather than an exclusive choice between two national attachments.
Return, Memory, and the Historical Limits of Reconciliation
The materials examined in this section demonstrate that the possibility of returning to Cuba cannot be reduced to a single emotional or political process. In
55 hermanos

, childhood memories, familiar landscapes, and family reunions make visible the personal dimensions of separation. Testimonies about adaptation to American society and participation in political movements reveal how some emigrants developed interpretations different from those associated with earlier exile narratives. Through the Antonio Maceo Brigade, these experiences became connected to an organized initiative that made renewed contact with Cuba possible under historically specific conditions.
The later testimonies in
Ecos del Exilio

demonstrate that the questions raised by the Brigade did not disappear with its initial visits. Family convictions could remain influential without determining every descendant's choices. Attachments to Cuba could endure alongside lives established elsewhere, while the desire for return did not necessarily guarantee acceptance or recognition. These accounts document different positions rather than successive stages of a universal diasporic experience.
The historical significance of
55 hermanos

also depends on recognizing the limitations of its representation. Its scenes of emotional arrival and reunification offer evidence of encounters and experiences articulated by particular participants, but they do not establish that the entire Cuban emigrant population welcomed renewed relations with the island. Its political narrative must be examined in relation to the institutional circumstances of ICAIC production. Likewise, the testimonies selected in
Ecos del Exilio
cannot stand for all Cubans residing in Puerto Rico. Each documentary participates in the public representation of migration through a different historical and narrative position.

Taken together, these audiovisual sources reveal return as a relationship between memory, political experience, family obligations, and the possibility of renewed contact. A journey to Cuba could bring people into the presence of places and relatives they had long remembered, but it could not undo the years of separation or guarantee that the meanings assigned to the past would be shared. Within the broader history of Cuban migration to Puerto Rico, return therefore becomes part of the continuing negotiation of belonging rather than the conclusion of exile. The community's history emerges through these changing relationships, including the disagreements over who could return, under what circumstances, and what that encounter might mean.
